# Object Systems: What Kind of OOP S7 Is

## Two traditions of object orientation

Object-oriented programming is not one idea but at least two, and R is unusual
in making both traditions ordinary parts of package design. The distinction
matters because it changes what the design must name, where extension lives,
and which intuitions transfer safely from other languages.

The **message-passing tradition** descends from Smalltalk through C++, Java,
Python, and JavaScript. Objects encapsulate state and behavior together; you
send a message to an object (`obj.method(arg)`) and the object decides how to
respond. The class is the unit of organization: it owns its methods, controls
access to its fields, and behavior extension means subclassing or mixins. In R
this tradition is represented by R6 (and the older Reference Classes), where
objects are environments with attached functions and genuine mutable state.

The **generic-function tradition** descends from CLOS (the Common Lisp Object
System) through Dylan and Julia. Here classes define *data and identity* while
behavior lives in **generic functions** — ordinary-looking functions that
select an implementation (a *method*) based on the classes of their arguments.
A method call looks like any function call: `speak(dog)`, not `dog.speak()`.
S3, S4, and S7 are all in this family; the S7 documentation calls it
"functional OOP." From the outside, behavior remains function application and
composes naturally with R's functional style: values flow through ordinary
calls and pipes, methods remain implementations of verbs rather than hidden
entries in an object's method table, and packages can add behavior without
owning the class definition.

The philosophical difference matters for design. In message-passing OOP, the
central design question is "what objects exist and what do they encapsulate?"
In generic-function OOP it splits in two: "what *is* each thing?" (classes,
properties, invariants) and "what can be *done*, and to which things?"
(generics and their methods). A well-designed S7 system co-designs its nouns
and verbs. A deliberately curated **verb vocabulary** — its generics —
matters as much as the class graph. This is the important correction to
class-centered habits: drawing a complete inheritance tree and only then
asking what users need to do designs half an interface.

Consider a family of document nodes. A class-first design may distinguish
nodes only by stored fields. Asking for `render()`, `references()`, and
`rewrite()` methods can reveal that two structurally similar nodes obey
different laws, while two structurally different nodes participate in the
same protocol. Operations reveal distinctions the representation is missing;
representations reveal useful dispatch axes and behavioral laws. The process
therefore iterates: classes do not need to be finished before methods inform
them, and a generic should name a stable domain action rather than expose the
current storage layout.

The two traditions also produce different extension stories. In
message-passing OOP, adding behavior normally means changing a class or a
subclass under its control. In generic-function OOP, another package can
define a new generic for existing classes or a new method for an existing
generic and a new class. That openness is powerful, but it makes generic
names, dispatch arguments, fallback behavior, and method laws part of the
public architecture.

## The landscape of R object systems

Choosing among R's systems is therefore not a syntax preference. The useful
distinctions are representation contract, operation model, and lifecycle. A
vector that must recycle correctly, a value whose construction establishes
invariants, and a session whose aliases must observe the same changes have
different semantics even if each could be forced into a class-shaped API.

**S3** is the lingua franca: an object is any value with a `class` attribute,
and `UseMethod()` dispatches on it. There are no formal fields, no validation,
no guarantees — only conventions. Its virtues are near-zero ceremony and
universal ecosystem reach (every `print`, `format`, `summary` in existence).
Its vice is that nothing stops anyone from constructing garbage. S3 remains the
right choice for lightweight interoperability wrappers, and it is the substrate
that vctrs disciplines.

**S4** provides explicit class definitions, typed slots, validity methods, and
multiple dispatch. It remains important in Bioconductor and other established
ecosystems. S7 pursues many of the same goals with a more regular interface
and explicit interoperability with existing systems.

**R6** provides message-passing OOP with reference semantics: objects are
mutable, methods are attached, `$clone()` exists because copies are no longer
automatic. R6 is not a competitor to S7; it answers a different question
(identity and mutation) and appears *alongside* S7 in well-designed packages.

**Environments** are the raw material of reference semantics — mutable bags
with identity — useful for caches and registries when R6's structure would be
overhead.

**vctrs** is not an object system so much as a rigorous S3 framework for
*vector* types: it supplies the algebra of sizes, prototypes, casting, and
coercion that makes a custom vector behave correctly in `c()`, `[`,
`data.frame` columns, and joins. If the thing you are modeling is
fundamentally a column of homogeneous values, vctrs is the answer and S7 is
not; re-implementing coercion rules in S7 validators is wasted, buggy effort.

**S7**, finally: formal classes with typed, validated, defaulted properties;
class validators for whole-object invariants; single and multiple dispatch via
generics; explicit `S7::super()`; declared compatibility with S3 and S4 in both
directions.

## What is distinctive about S7 itself

Several S7 design decisions reward close attention because they enable
patterns that S3/S4 made awkward.

**Classes are first-class values.** `S7::new_class()` returns an object that *is
simultaneously the class definition and its constructor*. You call it to make
instances; you pass it around like any value; you store it in lists; you write
functions that *return classes*. This makes class factories and registries
possible in ordinary R. They are useful when generated from an owned,
coherent specification or demonstrated repetition; first-class classes do not
by themselves justify generating a native class for every piece of foreign
structure.

A practical use is a parser registry whose wire tags select constructors:

```r
node_classes <- list(
  query = QueryNode,
  relation = RelationNode
)

construct_node <- function(input) {
  constructor <- node_classes[[input$type]]
  if (is.null(constructor)) {
    cli::cli_abort("Unknown node type {.val {input$type}}.")
  }
  do.call(constructor, input$fields)
}
```

The registry is data, so packages can inspect, extend, or test it without
encoding the same choice in a `switch()` at every boundary. This is most
useful when the tags and constructors belong to one coherent model; it is not
a reason to manufacture classes for distinctions the domain does not use.

The same fact supports useful *reflection* in ordinary R code. A tool can walk
class and generic metadata to report declared properties, parents, defaults,
validators, methods, and dispatch information. The
[datarr/reflect](https://github.com/SanD94/datarr) package does exactly this —
descriptor objects for properties, methods, and callables, with
method tables enumerated per generic and S7's own `S7::method_explain()` attached
as a dispatch trace. The boundary is important: an arbitrary validator is
executable code, not automatically inspectable constraint data. Documentation,
schemas, and forms can be projected only from metadata and constraints the
model represents explicitly. Those projections still require tests for
agreement.

**Properties have a full lifecycle.** A property is not just a typed slot. It
carries a class (which may be a union), a default (which may be a *quoted
expression* evaluated at construction — the standard trick for required
properties is `default = quote(stop("Required"))`), an optional validator, and
optional getter/setter for computed or guarded access. This is the layer where
most fine-grained design happens, and it is examined throughout
[Types and Meaning](03-types-and-meaning.qmd) and
[Parse, Don't Validate](04-parse-dont-validate.qmd).

**Validation is built into the object lifecycle.** Class validation runs at
construction and after supported property replacement, and a validator may
return a character vector describing several problems. The resulting
certificate is bounded by what the validator can see and by mutation paths:
reference-valued payloads can change behind the wrapper without triggering
outer validation. The consequences are developed in
[Parse, Don't Validate](04-parse-dont-validate.qmd).

**Dispatch is explicit and disciplined.** Generics declare their dispatch
arguments; method signatures are checked for compatibility against the generic
(a method missing an argument the generic promises produces a warning; a
method without `...` refuses misspelled arguments instead of silently
swallowing them, a real S3 footgun). `S7::super(x, to = Parent)` replaces the
implicit `NextMethod()` with an explicit statement of *which* parent behavior
you want. Multiple dispatch exists (`S7::new_generic(dispatch_args = c("x",
"y"))`) and, while rare, is decisive where behavior genuinely depends on two
types at once — serializing a value *for a dialect*, converting *from* one
type *to* another, combining two objects. The special classes `class_any` and
`class_missing` round out multiple dispatch by matching anything and
matching an absent argument respectively.

**Compatibility is bidirectional.** S7 methods can be registered on S3
generics; S3 and S4 classes can serve as property types (an S4 class via
`methods::getClass()`, an S3 class via `S7::new_S3_class()`); S7 classes can have
methods on S4 generics. This matters strategically: adopting S7 does not fence
you off from the ecosystem, and hybrid designs (an S7 property holding a DBI
S4 connection, an S7 class fronted by an S3 facade) are supported rather than
hacked.

## Choosing the substrate: a semantic decision procedure

The question "S7 or something else?" is answered by the semantics of the thing
being modeled. The following inventory is deliberately ordered: lifecycle and
vector behavior are harder to bolt on after the fact than a prettier print
method.

1. **Is it fundamentally a vector** — a column of homogeneous values that
   must slice, concatenate, recycle, and live in data frames? Then vctrs,
   possibly *held by* an S7 object but not replaced by one.

2. **Does it have identity and a lifetime** — a conversation, a connection, a
   cache, an accumulating log — where two references to it must observe each
   other's changes? Then reference semantics: R6 or an environment. An S7
   value may *snapshot* it, but the live thing is a reference.

3. **Is it a domain value** — a fact, configuration, document, message, or
   measurement — with nominal meaning, internal laws, or behavior worth
   dispatching on? Then S7 is a strong candidate. If an external metadata
   registry already owns the contract and no additional semantic identity is
   needed, an S3 value plus metadata may remain the better design.

4. **Is it a veneer** over something that already works, needed only so a
   `print` method looks right? Then S3, and stop there.

The procedure is not a tournament with one winner. The most instructive
designs use several systems at once, on purpose. In
ellmer, the `Chat` object is R6 because a conversation is an ongoing process
with identity — you append turns to *it* — while each `Turn` inside it is an
S7 value representing a record. Whether that value is editable or exposed as
a read-only snapshot is a separate API policy. In ragnar,
`MarkdownDocumentChunks` is an S7 class that *inherits from tibble*: the data
is fundamentally tabular (so it should behave as a data frame) but carries a
`@document` property and domain identity on top. These are not compromises;
they are the point. The systems are tools with distinct semantics, and fluency
means combining them without ideology.

## The expression problem, briefly

Generic-function OOP has a distinctive relationship to what Philip Wadler
named the expression problem [@wadler1998]: the difficulty of adding both new
data variants and new operations to a system without modifying existing code.
The problem explains why verb-centered extension is more than a calling
style. Class-owned
methods make new variants easy (subclass) and new operations hard (edit every
class). Pattern-matching functional code makes new operations easy (new
function) and new variants hard (edit every match). Generic functions make
*both* directions open: anyone can add a class and register methods for
existing generics; anyone can add a generic and register methods for existing
classes. ellmer exploits exactly this: adding a new LLM provider means adding
a `Provider` subclass and registering methods on the existing generic
vocabulary — no core changes.

The design opportunity is two-dimensional. A provider package can add a new
`Provider` variant to verbs ellmer already defines; an analysis package can
add a new operation over provider classes it does not own. Neither extension
requires turning the class into a God object or editing a central switch.
This is why an S7 API should expose a small, meaningful generic vocabulary:
those verbs are the joints at which independent packages can extend the
system.

The price of this openness is the absence of exhaustiveness checking: nothing
verifies at definition time that every variant handles every generic. An
abstract parent is not sealed, and a fallback method is not proof of coverage.
Loud fallbacks plus tests that enumerate the known registry detect unsupported
cases without claiming that the family is closed. These techniques are
discussed in
[Composition and Dispatch](05-composition-and-dispatch.qmd).
